question: What are the two main parts of the human immune system?
explanation: Great job! The immune system has two main teams: innate immunity (the fast, born-with-it guards) and adaptive immunity (the smart specialists that learn to fight specific germs over time). You've got this! [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is the immune system so important for our survival?

options.A: It regulates the normal daily temperature of the human body
options.B: It digests food nutrients inside the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: It controls the production of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.D: It protects the body against harmful microorganisms in the environment

explanation: Spot on! Think of your immune system as your body's personal security guard, constantly working behind the scenes to shield you from harmful germs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which of these is part of the body's first line of defence?
explanation: You got it! Your skin and mucous membranes act like a brick wall at the gate, stopping germs from entering your body in the first place. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h2)

question: How does stomach acid help protect you from getting sick?

options.A: By coating the intestinal lining with a thick mucus
options.B: By destroying ingested bacteria and other microorganisms
options.C: By producing specific antibodies against food antigens
options.D: By stimulating the production of white blood cells

explanation: Exactly! The strong acid in your stomach acts like a harsh chemical bath that kills most of the germs you accidentally swallow with your food or water. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h2)

question: What chemical alarm is released by damaged tissues to make blood vessels open up during inflammation?
explanation: Well done! When cells get hurt, they release histamine. This chemical sounds the alarm, making blood vessels wider so white blood cells can rush easily to the rescue. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why does a hurt or infected part of the body become warm and swollen?

options.A: Destruction of local nerve endings by invading bacteria
options.B: Decreased cellular activity slowing down the local metabolism
options.C: Rapid clotting of blood inside the deep muscle layers
options.D: Increased blood flow and fluid movement into the tissue

explanation: Correct! When your body sends extra blood and fluid to fight a germ at an injury site, it naturally causes warmth, redness, and swelling. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which white blood cells are mainly responsible for making antibodies?
explanation: You nailed it! B-lymphocytes are the antibody factories of your immune system, churning out proteins that target specific invaders. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h4)

question: What makes adaptive immunity so special compared to innate immunity?

options.A: It relies entirely on physical barriers like unbroken skin layers
options.B: It responds instantly within the first few minutes of exposure
options.C: It creates specific immunological memory against specific pathogens
options.D: It requires no cellular coordination or chemical signaling

explanation: Spot on! Adaptive immunity never forgets. Once it fights a germ, it remembers it, so if that same germ attacks later, your body fights back much faster and stronger. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the main job of lymph nodes in the body?

options.A: To produce digestive enzymes for the stomach
options.B: To manufacture red blood cells for iron transport
options.C: To pump oxygenated blood directly to body tissues
options.D: To filter lymph fluid and trap foreign pathogens

explanation: Correct! Think of lymph nodes as security checkpoints along a highway, filtering out fluid and trapping any bad germs before they can spread. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why do your glands (lymph nodes) often swell up and feel tender when you have an infection?

options.A: The flow of lymph fluid has stopped completely due to local blockage
options.B: White blood cells are rapidly multiplying inside them to fight the invader
options.C: Red blood cells are accumulating in the tissue to repair damaged vessels
options.D: The local temperature has dropped below normal physiological levels

explanation: You got it! When germs are around, your white blood cells throw a massive training and multiplying party inside the nodes, making them temporarily swollen and tender. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which hormone, released when you are under long-term stress, tends to lower your immune response?
explanation: Well done! High cortisol from chronic stress acts like a brake on your immune system, which is why stressed students easily catch colds during exams! [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h6)

question: Why is a patient taking long-term steroid medications at a higher risk of getting infections?

options.A: Corticosteroids cause an immediate permanent loss of lymph nodes
options.B: The medication suppresses normal immune and inflammatory responses
options.C: The treatment increases the production of abnormal red blood cells
options.D: The drug directly destroys the protective outer layers of the skin

explanation: Spot on! Corticosteroids calm down inflammation, but in doing so, they also quiet down the immune system, making it harder to fight off everyday germs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h6)

question: Why might a patient with a weak immune system who has a severe infection not show typical pus or swelling?

options.A: Their skin is too tough for localized swelling to become visible
options.B: Their body temperature is always too low to allow fluid accumulation
options.C: Their circulatory system moves blood too fast for fluid to leak
options.D: They lack an adequate number of white blood cells to create an inflammatory response

explanation: You're doing great! Pus and swelling are signs that white blood cells are fighting hard. If a patient doesn't have enough white blood cells, that visible battle scene won't show up. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is often the most reliable early warning sign of an infection in a patient with a very weak immune system?
explanation: Correct! Since other classic signs like pus or heavy swelling might not show up, a slight rise in temperature is often your first big clue that an infection is brewing. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is considered the single most effective way to stop infections from spreading in a hospital or clinic?
explanation: Spot on! Simple, regular handwashing is the absolute number one tool we have to keep germs from jumping from patient to patient. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h8)

question: What food safety rule is most important for a patient with a severely weakened immune system?

options.A: Eat only thoroughly cooked foods and avoid raw fruits or unpasteurized dairy
options.B: Consume raw salads daily to increase natural vitamin and fiber intake
options.C: Eat street foods as long as they are served at room temperature
options.D: Drink fresh unpasteurized milk to boost beneficial gut bacteria

explanation: You got it! Raw foods and unpasteurized dairy can hide sneaky bacteria and parasites that a healthy body handles easily, but can overwhelm a weak immune system. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h8)
